description: We’re Reach for the Stars, a team combining storytelling and technology to help children explore space. Our interests span design, space exploration, and accessible education. We’re excited to inspire the next generation of explorers. Space has no limits and neither should curiosity.
summary:
Reach for the Stars Museum is an educational 3D game that introduces children ages 8–17 to space exploration through an interactive story. Guided by Echo, a robot companion, players explore NASA machines, solve puzzles, and uncover the stories behind the technology that helps us understand our universe.

The museum turns learning into an adventure, encouraging players to ask questions and discover how each machine contributes to space exploration. Instead of simply reading about these technologies, children explore them within a virtual world where their curiosity moves the story forward.

With 20 languages and read-aloud options, the game aims to make space education more accessible to young learners around the world. Our dream is to unite young space enthusiasts through storytelling and inspire the next generation of explorers. Space has no limits and neither should curiosity.
details:
Their missions ended. Their stories didn’t.

Reach for the Stars Museum is a 3D game that introduces children ages 8–17 to the NASA machines behind space exploration. Set in a museum with 20 machines across Moon, Mars, and Deep Space wings, it combines real mission information with a mystery players must solve.

Players arrive on a school field trip and explore the exhibits with Echo, their robot guide. During the day, they learn why each machine was built, what happened on its mission, and how its discoveries helped those that followed. At midnight, the museum’s doors rearrange themselves, and its Homecoming Signal breaks into pieces hidden with the machines. Players navigate the maze, solve riddles, and uncover mission stories to recover the pieces. The restored signal reveals Voyager 1’s Pale Blue Dot image, bringing the journey back to Earth.

NASA information is part of the gameplay. Players compare mission photographs with later orbital images, listen to NASA recordings, and answer questions about what they discover. A journal records the machines they meet. The game also connects space exploration to inventions, law, and health. Even the maze introduces a computer science concept: finding a solution can take more work than checking one.

The museum offers a guided daytime Learning Mode and a nighttime Game Mode with changing layouts and three difficulty levels. Its interface supports 20 languages, with full mission-story translation still in progress. Read-aloud options and accessibility settings give more children a way to participate.

We built the project with help from Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, using GitHub to manage the code and collaborate. NASA mission information and media provided the foundation for the exhibits.

Not every child is drawn to space through a textbook or a list of mission dates. A robot guide or a secret room might give them a reason to start exploring. We hope players leave remembering a machine they had never heard of and wanting to learn what came after it.
